failure_summary.description: Agents chose contextually salient associated items without verifying that they matched the clue’s exact referent, category, and relation.
Agents expanded customary short answer forms into fuller personal or corporate names.

patch.reasoning: The existing semantic-type and exact-relation guidance already covers the first two failures, so repeating it is unwarranted. The name guidance, however, overweights full forms supplied by context and does not distinguish a familiar public brand from a longer corporate name. These edits clarify when a shorter conventional designation is the appropriate answer.

edits.target: For people, use the full identity supported by substantive context; do not answer with only a surname merely because a clue echo abbreviates it. Preserve initials, titles, and other name elements when the clue or a reliable passage supplies them—do not strip them for stylistic normalization.
edits.content: For people, use the name form conventional for the answer slot. Give the full identity when the clue asks for it or when needed to distinguish the person; otherwise, an established surname, mononym, or stage name can be the appropriate answer. Do not expand a familiar answer form merely because context supplies a fuller name, and retain initials, titles, or other elements when they are part of the requested conventional name.

edits.target: For proper names and titles, use the conventional form that identifies the requested entity. Do not substitute a nickname or later brand name for the historically relevant label, omit words from a work's title when the work is requested, or add optional middle names. Conversely, when the clue requests a generic class, do not embellish it with a narrower associated name.
edits.content: For proper names and titles, use the conventional form that identifies the requested entity at the clue's scope and in its historical or contextual frame. When a clue asks for a company or brand by its familiar public name, do not expand that name into a longer corporate name or append a product-category word just because a source uses it. Do not substitute a nickname or later brand name for a historically relevant label, omit words intrinsic to a requested work's title, or add optional middle names. Conversely, when the clue requests a generic class, do not embellish it with a narrower associated name.
